newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Trelleborg to list Boliden in Canada.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Trelleborg to list Boliden in Canada.

text.p: Swedish mining and rubber company Trelleborg AB said on Wednesday it was spinning off its mining unit Boliden, as widely speculated by the market, listing it in Canada alongside key international mining houses.
Trelleborg said the Toronto listing was likely to happen in June this year and the company would sell off about 50 percent of its stake with Trelleborg shareholders given preference.
"This was no surprise as the rumours had been around in the market for a couple of weeks now and the share price has risen strongly on this," said analyst Claes Vikbladh at Ohman.

"But it was not expected they would sell 50 percent. It was seen as more likely they would distribute 50 or even 100 percent to the shareholders," he said. "The big question now is what price they'll get with a range of five-12 billion crowns ($675 million-$1.62 billion)."
Trelleborg, which released a 1996 earnings report in line with market expectations as it announced the Boliden listing, closed two crowns higher at 119.5 crowns.
"I think it is positive that Trelleborg is trying to unlock its conglomerate structure," Fiba analyst Jan Dworsky said.
"But it very much depends now on what the company decides to do with the cash. I think it is important they do something with it otherwise they could find (themselves) being a holding company."

Trelleborg said the newly-listed company would probably be called Boliden Ltd and include business areas Mining and Metals, which means the Boliden company as well as interest companies Norzink and SCPM.
Boliden's current managing director Anders Bulow will head the listed company which aimed to push for a quick and strong expansion of mining operations.
"The expansion will primarily be directed towards an internationalisation by establishing operations in North and South America among others," Trelleborg said in a statement.
The strategy also includes plans to extend the Ronnskar copper mine in Sweden and explore other Swedish prospects.
Trelleborg said the listing would give Boliden better chances to finance investments.

"The listing in Toronto will be seen as an important industrial step in making Boliden an international company," managing director Kjell Nilsson said. "Trelleborg will remain the largest owner of Boliden."

Boliden is seen as a small fry in the mining world with annual turnover of about eight billion crowns. Analysts said it was likely Boliden, after listing, would need some kind of issue to raise enough money to finance its investment plans.
Dworsky said Boliden would probably do better on the Toronto exchange than in Sweden where it had not performed that well before it was taken over by Trelleborg 11 years ago.
"I think it'll get a fairer evaluation in Canada than in Sweden where it was like the odd one out," he said.
The Boliden news came with Trelleborg's 1996 report.

Trelleborg posted a profit after financial items, excluding restructing costs, of 1.02 billion crowns as forecast by the market compared with 1.55 billion in 1995. Sales fell to 20.57 billion crowns from 21.30 billion.
"The only disappointment was that despite the sell off of Boliden, the company kept the dividend unchanged at three crowns," said Vikbladh.
($1=7.41 crowns)
